extraction_text: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma about the merits of not eating meat and the sins of eating meat according to dharma.
Bhishma acknowledges that meat is delicious and beneficial for the weak, sick, or tired, and that nothing surpasses it in nutrition.

attributes.action: Agrees with Yudhishthira's observation about meat's appeal and utility

extraction_text: Bhishma states that not eating meat brings great merit, as harming other beings for one's own gain is cruel and sinful, and life is precious.
Bhishma explains that dharma is characterized by non-killing, but meat used in ancestral and divine rituals, as per Vedic rules, is purified and sinless to eat.

attributes.action: Cites Vedic scriptures for ritual meat consumption

extraction_text: Bhishma outlines rules for Kshatriyas: eating meat obtained through personal valor is sinless, and hunting is respected as deer were purified by Sage Agastya for gods.

attributes.action: Justifies hunting and meat-eating for warriors based on tradition and risk

extraction_text: Bhishma concludes that compassion for all beings is universally valued, and compassionate people are fearless.

attributes.action: Affirms the importance of compassion across times

extraction_text: The text discusses the virtues of compassion and non-violence, stating that compassionate people and ascetics possess both this world and the future world.
It describes how those who grant fearlessness to all beings are considered compassionate, and in return, all beings will protect them from harm.
The text explains that no creature can harm someone who has helped others escape difficulties, as they will be rescued when misfortune strikes.
It states that no gift is greater than granting life, and nothing is more precious than one's own life, emphasizing the universal fear of death.
The text describes the suffering of beings in the cycle of rebirth, including torment in the womb and repeated falls into hells.
It teaches that pure-hearted, self-controlled individuals develop compassion for all beings, and those who avoid meat from birth will attain heaven.
The text presents the law of karma: those who kill will be killed, those who bind will be bound, and those who eat meat will be eaten in return.
It extols non-violence (ahimsa) as the highest dharma, greatest strength, best friend, and most sacred revelation, surpassing all other religious acts.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma about the fate of warriors who die in battle, questioning why death is difficult for all people regardless of their circumstances.
Bhishma explains that all living beings experience birth and endless cycles of rebirth, then promises to answer Yudhishthira's question by recounting a past story.
Bhishma begins the story of Sage Vyasa (also called Krishna Dvaipayana or Island-born) encountering a worm on a road.

supernatural_elements: Vyasa understands animal/species languages and knows all beings' fates in rebirth

extraction_text: Vyasa sees a worm quickly crawling away from the middle of a road used by vehicles and questions it about its fear and destination.

attributes.action: Vyasa questions the worm about its behavior

extraction_text: The worm explains it is frightened by the loud noise of approaching vehicles, fearing being crushed, and values its life despite being a lowly creature.

attributes.action: Worm expresses fear of death and attachment to life

extraction_text: Vyasa questions whether the worm truly experiences happiness as a lowly creature and suggests death might be better for it.

attributes.action: Vyasa challenges the worm's claim of happiness

extraction_text: The worm responds that all living beings find contentment in their circumstances, so even as a worm, it feels happiness.

attributes.theme: Contentment with one's existence regardless of form

actions: Served its old mother with respect

extraction_text: A Kshatriya who performed his duties with pride will be reborn as a Brahmin. A virtuous Brahmin can enjoy heavenly bliss.

attributes.context: From the Mahabharata's Shanti Parva, Chapter 119

extraction_text: After being freed from the worm body, the being was reborn as a powerful Kshatriya who performed Kshatriya duties. He remembered his past lives and began practicing difficult austerities.
The Brahmin sage Krishna Dvaipayana (Vyasa) visited the Kshatriya who was practicing austerities.

Vyasa instructed the Kshatriya that his vow should be to protect all beings, and by doing so while practicing self-restraint and righteousness, he could become a Brahmin after abandoning his Kshatriya body.

attributes.key_advice: Protect subjects, practice self-restraint, follow dharma to become Brahmin

extraction_text: The Kshatriya returned to the forest, followed Vyasa's teachings, and protected his subjects according to dharma.
After some time, the Kshatriya died and attained Brahmin status due to faithfully protecting his subjects.
Vyasa visited the being again after he had become a wise and famous Brahmin.
Vyasa told the Brahmin that he would no longer suffer, that each person reaches their destination based on their actions, and that he should now only worry about straying from dharma.

attributes.key_message: Karma determines rebirth, focus on following highest dharma

extraction_text: The being (formerly the worm) thanked Vyasa for helping him progress from happiness to greater happiness, eliminating his sins, and establishing his happiness in dharma.

attributes.result: Merged with Brahman, reached Brahma's world

extraction_text: Bhishma concluded to Yudhishthira that excellent Kshatriyas should die on the battlefield to attain auspicious destinations, so Yudhishthira shouldn't grieve for them.

attributes.key_message: Kshatriyas dying in battle attain good destinations
